title: The desert houses
hookLine: Carmelites keep times of deep silence and solitude

cards: Mark's Gospel describes a long day in Capernaum. Jesus heals a fever, and by sunset the whole town seems to be crowded at the door with its sick.

Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." His friends come hunting for him, and when they find him, they say it plainly: "All seek for thee."
Before the next town, before the next crowd, he goes to a quiet place first. Carmelites took that pattern and gave it buildings.

teach.b: A desert, in Carmelite language, doesn't need sand.
It's a place set apart for silence and solitude.

In the reformed branch of the order, friars founded houses they called deserts, set apart from busy places, where a friar could withdraw for a season and live closer to the hermits of the first Carmel: a cell, long hours of prayer, very little talk.
The idea comes straight out of the Rule from a few days ago. The Rule asks for silence, and it quotes the prophet Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "in silence and in hope shall your strength be."
Silence there isn't emptiness. It's where strength is gathered. The prophet Hosea gives the desert a tenderness, too.

teach.h: I WILL SPEAK TO HER HEART.
teach.b: God says of his people: "I will allure her, and will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart." The wilderness is where the speaking happens, because nothing else is talking.
Some Carmelite communities still keep desert days and times of deeper retreat, and lay people who follow Carmel sometimes make their own. Notice the rhythm, though.

teach.h: INTO THE DESERT, THEN BACK OUT.
teach.b: Jesus goes to the desert place, and then he goes back out, to the next towns. The desert isn't an escape from people.

teach.h: IN SILENCE AND IN HOPE SHALL YOUR STRENGTH BE.
teach.b: It's a return to the source, so there's something to give them. A desert house may be far away. But an hour without noise, a walk without headphones, a room with the door shut, can do a small version of the same work.

how: Carmelite communities keep regular times of deeper silence and solitude, sometimes called desert days, and some Carmelite friars have houses set apart for longer periods of retreat.

games.why: Mark says he rose very early, went into a desert place and prayed. when his friends found him, he went on to the next towns.

practice: Let everything go quiet for a little while: no music, no screen, no plans. If you pray, rest in Isaiah's words, in silence and in hope, and let God speak first; if you don't, just listen to how loud the quiet is.

wordCard.voice: The desert houses. Carmelite places set apart for deep silence and solitude, the hermit life of the first Carmel, kept alive. Today's word.
